comments.name: Jack Connolly
comments.body:
Trump may fancy himself a bare-knuckled political brawler, but nothing could be further from the truth.  At heart, Trump is a coward--physically, emotionally, intellectually, and politically.

There's a reason why his nickname is TACO--"Trump Always Chickens Out."  He never takes responsibility.  Wasn't that his mantra during his first administration?  Mistakes and missteps were someone else's fault, never his.

He doesn't have the stomach for a full-on political fight.  Add to that his advanced age and deteriorating mental faculties.  He's no longer the energetic outsider dropping insults in the 2016 GOP debates.  In the last years of his administration, Trump may not get chewed up by 2 or 3 Congressional wolves looking to make their bones before 2028, but he will get stung to death by 435 angry hornets who are tired of his incompetence and narcissism.

And let's not forget the elephant in the room (no pun intended): the war with Iran.  Of all the promises a Presidential candidate can make, "No more forever wars" hits home with everyone.  No parent wants to ship their son or daughter off to die in a foreign land, especially for a President who doesn't know how to wage a war or how to draw up a peace treaty.

Don't forget that gas rose from $2.99 a gallon in March to $4.29 a gallon in November.  All because Trump needed a war to distract the public from the Epstein files.  Trump is terrified of what is in those documents.  He deserves to be.  What did he do on that island?

comments.name: Andy
comments.body:
For years, Elon Musk has built his fortune on a simple formula: cultivate the powerful and let them open the federal checkbook. Billions in taxpayer dollars have flowed to his companies. Then he escalated, pouring staggering sums into Donald Trump’s and the Republican Party’s campaigns in the expectation that his investment would keep paying off in Washington.

What should trouble every citizen is how willing Republican leaders were to embrace him. They welcomed his money, and when Democrats sought to compel him to answer questions under oath, they blocked the effort. When one party shields the richest man in the world from scrutiny while his companies collect public contracts, the public interest comes last.

Voters have now shifted the balance of power in Congress, and with it the prospect of real oversight. Investigators should look hard at how his companies won contracts, what role DOGE played, and whether taxpayers were shortchanged through conflicts of interest, favoritism, or worse. That scrutiny is long overdue. Others who have treated the government as a private revenue stream should take notice.

comments.name: castaff
comments.body:
Democrats need to plan carefully what their next steps are. It's hard for Congress (or a president, for that matter) to lower prices. But first, they can help with the cost of living by restoring the Obamacare subsidies and Medicaid funding.

Second, given that concerns about corruption have finally emerged as major concerns, I'd like to see both houses of Congress hold some public hearings with cabinet members, White House staff, and the tech and energy industry executives - and maybe talk to some of the whistleblowers in the executive branch, Then, craft some sensible legislation that builds on existing restrictions (I'm retired federal civil service and had to disclose certain of my investments, etc. every year) to curb the outrageous self-dealing and insider trading in the White House and Congress. If Trump vetos it, well that's a big plank in the Democrats' 2028 presidential platform.

When I saw the tech bros arrayed behind Trump at his inauguration, I feared the worst. Sadly, the corruption has been even more blatant than my cynical self imagined. I'm glad many of my fellow Americans seem to agree. Time to rein them in, as well as undo the disastrous cuts imposed by the DOGE team.

I'm sure I speak for many, when I say enough is enough! I voted with that mindset, and voters handed Congressional power to the Democrats. Time to get to work, folks!

comments.name: Sconseter

I was so worried about 1) voter intimidation, through ICE or something else; 2) voting machine machinations (given that they're now owned by an extreme right-wing Republican); and 3) that Trump would just plain old reject the results.

comments.name: Deej

comments.name: Walter Stellenbosch

"Decency Won"

Don't get carried away. Voters did what they typically do: they chose the party and party candidates that they thought or felt would be best for them, their families, and their communities. 

Very few are the Americans in a position to place their thoughts or feelings about what's best for the country ahead of the more immediate concerns of average Americans.

comments.name: Mind of Reason

The Teump party was not punished.  It was repudiated.

comments.name: Fred Mueller
comments.body:
The mind says Iran, gas, groceries, and inflation …

But the heart revolts at cruelty, gross monuments,  misuse of the legal system,  appalling grift and self dealing and the pathological need for attention and praise.

comments.name: Alyson Lloyd
comments.body:
Friends,
My grandmother lived in Georgia before she died. I know she's happy those women were elected to office. They are a great example that Black women can climb to top of the mountain!

comments.name: Patti
comments.body: This election is a direct repudiation of the failed administration; who accomplished nothing except making all of our lives worse. The enrichment and corruption of the Trump family and cronies finally became too much for Americans to swallow.

comments.name: Cassandra

What legislative agenda would that be?  Disenfranchising more minority voters while enriching himself and his family?

comments.name: Captain Sanity

Tariffs on Canada and other allies need to be reversed but will the Dems see the money they raise and do it? We will see. articles.title: America Punishes Trump’s Party: 8 Takeaways From a Democratic Landslide

comments.name: LR
comments.body:
Unless and until they vote to ban insider trading by members of congress, and get corporate money out of elections, and ban lobbyists while they’re at it, they will risk being seen as hypocrites.

comments.name: ViewFromFarAway

To not insist that the rule of law and the Constitution be followed and that the criminality and corruption be punished is to ask for it to happen all over again. These are not crimes like jaywalking. This is siding with Putin. Waging an illegal war. Extreme corruption and grifting. The crimes detailed but redacted  in the Epstein files. comments.name: Twetti S

comments.name: Alan Knight
comments.body:
Watching the entire coverage from when the polls closed on the east coast to the point where Democrats got over the line in congress was definitely one of the most thrilling elections I've ever seen. (And I've been watching politics since the 1970s)

comments.name: Chris K
comments.body: I love your exchanges but please keep in mind that when it comes to predicting what will work in a presidential cycle, the truth is nobody knows anything.  Judging who it would or would not be a mistake as a party's nominee is a fraught exercise.  Don't forget that the worst possible person to be President in the entire country was nominated three times and won twice.  Also, as the commentariat seems to forget all too frequently, Presidential elections are between two people, not between one person and some theoretical opponent.  Would AOC be a terrible candidate?  Who knows?  Depends on who the Republican nominee would be.  JD?  He's the most unlikable, awkward politician this century.  I think she might do well against him.  Tucker Carlson?  That matchup might result in a total realignment of the electorate since many of their positions would overlap but the ones that don't would be about as different as they could be.  Ron DeSantis?  Tim Scott?  Who knows?  Also, just as an aside, interesting that neither of you thought to mention that Jon Ossoff is Jewish.  How about an Ossoff-El Sayed ticket? comments.name: J Collins
comments.body: "We have no history of major disagreements." I doubt it. We are only getting one side of the story. I'm not summarily blaming the parent, but it seems unlikely that after one disagreement that an adult child who agreed to stay with her for some of the time after surgery would break off contact over this. More likely it has been a toxic relationship for decades that the daughter has put up with, but can't continue forever in that way. She has her own family now and her spouse and children need to be the priority, not maintaining a stressful toxic relationship. The mom is probably lucky total estrangement hasn't happened, and sooner. While people romanticize multi-generational families in multiple cultures, the reality is that we live in much more complex and mentally stressful times, and for much longer. Putting up with that kind of toxicity indefinitely is certainly not normal, and nothing the daughter is obliged to do. I think that the advice given by Galanes is good. Eventually, the daughter will probably be willing to have some communication, but the reality is sometimes cutting the proverbial phone cord is the only thing that toxic parents will respond to.

comments.name: Katie
comments.body: I think PG is right-on with his advice. LW would be honoring her daughter's condition to rebuild their relationship by going to therapy. I'm not saying the daughter was being fair or reasonable here, but LW owes it to herself to interrogate if any of her own unconscious behaviors or biases contributed to their damaged relationship. Maybe she'll come away able to express her feelings less antagonistically.

comments.name: Clare
comments.body: It bothers me that when there are letters about estranged children and parents, everyone heaps onto the parent. But adult relationships go in both directions. The daughter’s refusal to go to family counseling suggests that she places all the blame on her mother, and none of the responsibility on herself. With my own mother’s recent surgeries, she was dependent on me for weeks, and my leaving would have been a kind of betrayal. It’s obvious that the mother is responsible for repairing this relationship, but she can only do so much on her own. I hope he daughter eventually realizes that she has to contribute as well.

comments.body:
LW, this daughter will sadly reap what she sows later looking back, when she learns life is very short and her own children are older and her mother is not around. NC should be reserved for extreme cases--not a weapon to wield in our most important relationships.
disagree if you must, but i stand by this.

Many  young people now feel this is an acceptable and viable option in resolving family conflict.   The attitudes and beliefs of the children who are cutting off contact are markedly different than previous generations.  Psychologists have identified this as a trend, and research is being conducted  to better understand how and why this is occurring with frequency.  

I would advise the mother to go into therapy, for herself.  I do not agree that her daughter has handled this appropriately,

comments.name: Tall Trees and Trains
comments.body: When reading these; and for reasons I am no entirely sure, I do enjoy reading them; I can't but help but feel like many of them are people just trying to feel validated for making a choice they want to make.

comments.name: Helen
comments.body:
LW1: So, your daughter is a busy mom of four, but agreed to take care of you post-surgery for two weeks, but... had to step away for some of that period? This feels like we're missing some information. Was she meant to be a full-time caretaker? Why was she stepping away -- for a vacation, or to take care of her large and busy family? Was she supposed to drop everything for you?

You snapped at her and apologized -- good! Is this a pattern? How often do you snap at her? How often do you expect her to drop everything for you? What, in your eyes, is a "major" disagreement? Hardly anyone goes as far as no contact out of nowhere. Why did you suggest therapy? I am of the opinion that therapy is a good thing, but if you felt this was no big deal, this seems like an odd jump. Did you say "I want to fix our relationship," or was it more like "you need therapy to get over your problem?" 

I am someone who cut off my own mother after years and years of telling her what she was doing and why it was hurting me. She never listened. If she had, I wouldn't have cut her off. If your daughter won't talk to you, the best thing you can do is respect her wishes and boundaries and show you're taking her seriously. Then, maybe, she'll be willing to talk.

comments.name: Sasha
comments.body: My mother and father are covert narcissists.  I have been no contact (NC in narc survivor community lingo) for the past 4 years.  Going NC was a painful journey navigated through talk therapy and psychiatric care.  It is the right decision to protect my mental health.  I will not heal if I am exposed to the deception, duplicity, gaslighting, and general disregard for what I want my life to look like as an independent adult.  My pain as a result of my parents' treatment of me did not surface until my 30s; I am in middle age now.  To the child I urge you to start talk therapy and to learn about narcissism.  Dr. Ramani, Jerry Wise, Patrick Teahan, Blake Anderson are helpful sources of research I found on YouTube concurrent to my talk therapy.  As a child of narc parents, through the hard work of healing from their abuse, I learned that I was in denial for so many years.  The reason is that we are biologically programmed to want to please our parents; it is a survival tool.  To undo this element of our DNA is a long and tiring process.  To the parent who is writing, if you are able to be truly honest with yourself, look in the mirror and ask yourself how much of your parenting was done for your child's benefit or for yours?

A good houseguest makes no demands, and helps with the meals, and cleanup. Do treat the host to dinner or lunch.   

We had "the man who came to dinner' whose demands were burdensome, endless, and a klutz who broke stuff.  He brought no housewarming gifts, and a disrupted our life.  Friendship eventually ended not over his houseguest behavior: it was a symptom of his selfishness. 

If you are not set up to have houseguests, very private, or a nervous host, have no bed in the spare rooms.  If you get grief or guilt by saying no, it is time to move on. You are just being used. 

David Philly

In 1973 Rittel and Webber characterized the 'wickedly hard' problems that are of central interest to humans and their institutions:
• There is no definitive formulation of a wicked problem.
• Wicked problems have no stopping rule.
• Solutions to wicked problems are not true-or-false, but good-or-bad.
• There is no immediate and no ultimate test of a solution to a wicked problem.
• Every solution to a wicked problem is a ‘one-shot operation’; because there is no opportunity to learn by trial-and-error, every attempt counts significantly.
• Wicked problems do not have an enumerable (or an exhaustively describable) set of potential solutions, nor is there a well-described set of permissible operations that may be incorporated into the plan.
• Every wicked problem is essentially unique.
• Every wicked problem can be considered to be a symptom of another problem.
• The existence of a discrepancy representing a wicked problem can be explained in numerous ways. The choice of explanation determines the nature of the problem’s resolution.
• The planner has no right to be wrong.

Anthropic and its rivals are already lost in this thicket, this real-world turbulence in which humans and their institutions thrive and suffer. These are not 'scaling problems'  to be solved by more-of-the-same tactical finesse. The Armardas of 'Rationalism,' the Tech Bro flavor or otherwise, founder on the shoals of these hard realities.

The fact that Alito (and Thomas) won't retire despite the fact that the Senate is functionally locked down as Democratic until 2033 is evidence that suggests the court and the Justices (even the ones you don't like) are not as partisan as they are portrayed in this publication and in the media generally. If he rushed to retire in the next few months, that would be a very different story, but that is the opposite of what is being reported here. 

While I agree with ethical standards being enacted at the Court, this exact situation is why we should actually NOT have term limits. Can you imagine if a Presidential candidate knew they would get to replace a Justice in the upcoming election? It would politicize the Court in a horrible way and turn it into another useless branch like all of Congress whose members are just aura farming for Instagram likes. Elections would be about who candidates would get to nominate, and we would be far less likely to end up with people who put their jurisprudence before party.

1. Decisions are not taken in a vacuum, and dementia care is expensive. If the book may help pay for his care, that's a reasonable thing to consider. 

2. All authors who draw on their lives--that's to say, nearly all authors--run into this issue. Furthermore, any author can cobble together aspects of multiple people, real or imagined. Only you know how close you're hewing to your source material. Unless you're presenting the work as historically-precise autobiography (no details altered) the hand-wringing about lawsuits seems remote. 

3. He was convicted and served his time, thus the crime is a matter of public record that anyone (including a true crime story AI bot) could write about. It's the other more private aspects of the story that could more reasonably worry you. 

4. I am guessing that you intend the juxtaposition of the personal life and the public crime to create some sense of sympathy, and create shades of gray in a discourse about crime and mental illness. If so, you are retroactively doing your brother a service. That also belongs in the calculation. (If you're mostly patting yourself on the back for being a good sibling, or flagellating yourself for not being a better one, this does not apply.)

5. Unless you're putting words and thoughts into your brother's head, you are writing about your own life. Not his. And the writers' classic credo is that telling your own lived experience is, and must remain, your absolute right.

In college, the psychology department I was engaged in focused on behaviorism. B.F. Skinner investigated what he believed were the foundations of behavior, the relationship between a stimulus and a response. 

Like other undergraduates grounded in the humanities, I found Skinners' approach dangerously reductive. As time has passed, though, Skinner's insights have proved to have a place.  

My objections to AI rest squarely on the dangers of accelerated global warming. But the dangers of addiction, of which behaviorism gave us the first animal model, follow close behind. Instant gratification of any kind is addictive. Our personal will and agency are exploitable. 

Screen time is addictive, as are all pleasure inducing stimuluses that in earlier times, we had to work hard for. 

With AI we no longer need to think, or paint, or read. We become tied to our digital leashes. I wonder how, in the future, we are going to combat the "expertise" of a sophisticated device when the data it has been fed or the conclusions it reaches are fundamentally wrong for us. 

I actively resist AI. I no longer use Google, which does not allow a user to opt out. It may take a few more keystrokes to find what I am looking for, or take a risk to make a new friend, or muddle through the design of my own flyers, but those activities rewarding in and of themselves.

I may not be able to completely divest from AI, but I refuse to passively succumb to it.

The burden of proof for whatever we buy next has shifted 180 degrees: The question is now "why buy anything that includes an ICE", not "why buy an EV". We have plenty of charging resources in New England, we've never even come close to running out. We charge at home most of the time so it's very convenient, no more gas stations.

I will not buy anything from Elon, but I have been exceptionally satisfied with my GM offerings. Well priced, plenty of features, and extremely reliable. The RAV4 has had the most recalls of any of our fleet.

I also switched from oil heat to heat pump. We had already converted a smoothtop electric range to induction a few years back, it performs like gas ranges we had in the past. Most of our lawn/garden tools are now electric (corded or battery).

I'm not made of money. All of the above happened over more than a decade. The reality is that for plenty of use cases the electric stuff is close on cost (or if you go corded, often cheaper), no maintenance, high reliability, lighter, less stuff to break, and just overall better.

The reason Gandhi is important is because of what he accomplished, and what he advocated that we still need to do (undoubtedly not exactly in the ways he envisioned): environmentalism, localization of power (and resources), and returning to past ways of living, to some extent, when they were better (see: environmentalism). He had many insights from which we still need to learn.

Beyond that, he was far from perfect. We can stop pretending that he was a saint in that sense of being anywhere near flawless. But our current work isn't looking for saints--it's improving ourselves, adapting in an insightful way to our current (fairly dire) circumstances. While we don't want to paper over Gandhi's flaws, spending all or most of our time studying him focused on those flaws and rejecting his insights wastes our time. Which is typical--that is how we got into this environmental and social mess, misattributions of our priorities. His thinking still has enormous, compelling, radical value. What we really need to be doing is changing ourselves, and some of Gandhi's thought is an important tool for how to do that. If we're wasting time deciding where to hand out laurel crowns and where to hold them back, we're avoiding our own power and the real work.

The summer I turned 22, I rode my bicycle from Seattle--where I'd spent most of my childhood to age 8--to Boston--where I spent most of the remainder. Soon after finishing that ride, I wrote up my ride. Remembering that ride, and reading what I wrote about it both add joy to my day. 50 years after I took that ride, I'd love to do it again. I drank a lot of coffee on that trip, but then, coffee is something that has added joy to my day since my 3 years older brother convinced me to try it when I was around 12 or 13, when our family, on a road trip, was staying in a hotel in Chicago. 
My dog, a border collie, brings me joy. My close friends bring me joy. Driving my '08 Civic (5 on the floor) brings me joy. It's my favorite car that I've ever owned, because it's so much fun to drive. 
Reading brings me joy. A particular example: probably at least two decades ago, I read Sebastian Junger's Tribe--a book that examines the conditions under which H. sapiens are our best selves.  Later, I read Endurance: Shackleton's Incredible Voyage (or something like that) in which Antarctic ice chews up Shackleton's boat, ruining it, but he and his men nonetheless ultimately make it back to civilization under exceptionally difficult conditions, in no small part because they were able to work together so well, demonstrating the truth of what Sebastian Junger has to say in Tribe.

comments.body: The growing opposition to data center development should concern anyone who wants America to remain a world leader in technology. AI is likely to transform virtually every sector of our economy, but that future requires infrastructure, and data centers are an essential part of it. Concerns about electricity, water consumption, and noise are legitimate. Developers should be required to address these issues and demonstrate that their projects won't burden existing consumers, threaten local water supplies, or disrupt residential neighborhoods. But responsible regulation should not become an excuse to block development altogether. If we make it too difficult to build this infrastructure, other countries, particularly China, will gladly fill the void. We've already seen the consequences of allowing critical industries and supply chains to move overseas, as our dependence on foreign rare earth minerals demonstrates. We should not repeat that mistake with AI. We can protect our communities and natural resources while making America the world's leading destination for AI development. Let's not allow fear and short-term thinking to cost us our technological leadership.

What I do is film the progress of building and operating my haunted house - whether that be unboxing the animatronics, filming updates on construction, and tips and tricks for others who want to follow in my footsteps. The online community loves watching it, and all of the people who visit love the experience as well. It’s a win-win-win! I’m happy, and so are my physical and online supporters. I look forward to designing it every year, and the public looks forward to what I design. If you can get money while doing what you love, PLUS be able to put that money right back into what you love, it just creates a timeless pastime that I can’t get enough of.

comments.name: Tim Barrus
comments.body: Science fiction is difficult to review. The genre is so dependent on stereotypes. They are dominating every new science fiction novel I am reading. I am sometimes forgiving twice. I find that science fiction writers can come up with a great first sentence, and a great first page. That is because we are all told by the agent community they will not work with us unless we can perform that particular hat trick. That is when the whole enterprise becomes a dog and pony show. It's called the hook. Today's writers must create a hook because publishing is fishing. No editor will read your work unless you have a hook. All genre publishing is about following the rules. Publishings' rules and regulations do not bend. These are usually tight little anal minds and writing between the lines. The only thing more depressing than creating stereotypes is creating better stereotypes. I love science fiction. But I have to write my own books because I can't find anything that is more than the latitude and longitude of stock characters burdened with the caste marks of mileage tickets to places we have been before. Science fiction could be an art form that informs us and creates process itself -- one not set in stone -- but in isothermal lines of monograms where caricature is an extravagance. Writing science fiction is a bondage of business conventions that demand the ordinary and nothing but the ordinary. Once you submit science fiction, be prepared for the wannabe editors to tear it to shreds.
